title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context: in E297 Euler re-derives the Euler–Lagrange equation for ∫Z dx, with Z = Z(x,y,p,q,r,s,...) and p=y', q=y'', ..., using variations δy and integration by parts (§21). The first variation splits into two parts. One is an integral ∫δy(N − P' + Q'' − R''' + S'''' − ...)dx. The other is an 'absolute' (boundary) part at x=a: δy(P − Q' + R'' − S''' ...) + δy'(Q − R' + S'' ...) + δy''(R − S' ...) + ... The interior equation gives the Euler–Lagrange equation (§§23–25).

This page (§§25–28) explains what the boundary terms are for, and why the new method is better than the 1744 Methodus inveniendi, which gave only the interior equation.

§26: If Z = Z(x,y) only (P=Q=...=0), the boundary part vanishes identically and the condition N = ∂Z/∂y = 0 settles everything. Example: Z = bb − nxy + y³/c gives N = −nx + 3y²/c = 0, so y² = ncx/3. This is a pointwise stationarity problem with no arbitrary constants.

§27: If Z also contains p, the condition N − dP/dx = 0 is a differential equation, second order when P contains p. Its integration brings in one or two arbitrary constants. Euler had already noted in the 1744 treatise that one can prescribe y(a), and in the second-order case one further condition is left at our disposal.

§28: Among this family, which member gives the true extremum? The answer comes from the previously neglected boundary term, here Pδy, which must vanish at x=a. In general, when y(a), y'(a), ... are free, the following must hold at x=a:
- P − Q' + R'' − S''' + ... = 0
- Q − R' + S'' − ... = 0
- R − S' + ... = 0
- S = 0, etc.
In modern terms these are the natural (free-endpoint) boundary conditions for higher-order Lagrangians. The next page applies them to ∫√(1+p²)/√y dx. The condition p=0 at x=a gives the cycloid meeting the terminal vertical orthogonally, with b = a/π (the brachistochrone to a given vertical line).
errors: Euler treats only the upper end x=a as free. Boundary terms at the lower limit are tacitly dropped: the variation or the integral is implicitly assumed to vanish there, so the natural conditions at the initial point are not stated.

The full list of conditions at x=a applies only if y(a), y'(a), y''(a), ... are all free. If some of them are prescribed (as §27 allows for y(a)), only the conditions belonging to the free derivatives should be imposed. Euler's wording ('ulterius determinari') leaves this choice implicit.
In the §26 example, y² = ncx/3 is only a stationary point. Whether it is a maximum or a minimum depends on the sign of ∂²Z/∂y² = 6y/c, which is not discussed. This is minor.

ideas.what: Boundary ('absolute') terms of the first variation, after integration by parts, yield extra conditions at a free endpoint that select the extremal among the family left by the Euler–Lagrange equation.
ideas.modern_name: Natural boundary conditions / transversality conditions (free endpoint)
ideas.where_published: E296 Elementa calculi variationum and E297, Novi Comm. Petrop. 10 (1766); later in Institutiones calculi integralis vol. 3 appendix

ideas.what: General higher-order natural boundary conditions: P − Q' + R'' − ... = 0, Q − R' + ... = 0, ..., S = 0 at x=a.
ideas.modern_name: Natural boundary conditions for higher-order Lagrangians (as in beam theory: vanishing moment and shear at a free end)
ideas.where_published: E297 (this paper); Institutiones calculi integralis III appendix (E385)

ideas.what: Degenerate case where Z depends on x and y only: the extremum condition reduces to ∂Z/∂y = 0 pointwise (example y² = ncx/3).
Remark that the Euler–Lagrange equation of second order leaves constants free, so endpoint values can be prescribed.
ideas.modern_name: Boundary value problem for the Euler–Lagrange ODE

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard natural boundary conditions from the 1760s δ-calculus (Euler and Lagrange), well documented in the histories of the calculus of variations (e.g. Goldstine, Fraser) and in the Opera omnia. There is nothing new beyond the known content.
transcription_corrections: §26 example: the print reads '(bb−nxy+y³/c)dx'. The intended problem is ∫(bb−nxy+y³/c)dx; the integral sign is missing in the original typesetting, not a transcription error.
Otherwise the transcription matches the image: N = −nx + 3yy/c and yy = ⅓ncx are correct.
